domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: A monitor shows a chaotic baseline with no identifiable QRS complexes. What is the diagnosis and immediate treatment?
rationale: VF is lethal; the only definitive treatment is immediate DC cardioversion before irreversible cardiac death.
confusable_with: Artifact (check pulse, but treat as VF if pulseless)

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What rate range defines accelerated idioventricular rhythm and why is it generally benign?
answer: 40-100 bpm; often a reperfusion rhythm after coronary occlusion, usually transient and does not require treatment.
rationale: AIVR reflects escape rhythm emergence after reperfusion normalizes ischemia; it is typically self-limiting unlike true VT.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What QRS width on ECG defines a ventricular arrhythmia and what rate range characterizes ventricular tachycardia?
answer: Wide QRS >3 small boxes (>120 ms); VT rate is 120-200 bpm.
rationale: Wide QRS indicates origin below the AV node with aberrant ventricular conduction; rate differentiates AIVR from VT.
confusable_with: SVT with aberrancy (narrow origin but wide conduction)

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What are the ICD indications in ischemic and non-ischemic cardiomyopathy?
answer: Ischemic CM: EF <=30-35% with NYHA II-III; CRT if EF <=35% + prolonged QRS +/- LBBB.
rationale: ICD reduces sudden cardiac death risk in patients with severely reduced EF; CRT improves cardiac synchrony and may also reduce arrhythmia risk.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: How does tachycardia impair cardiac output in a patient with a stiff ventricle?
answer: Tachycardia reduces LV filling time, decreasing stroke volume and CO, especially in patients with poor compliance.
rationale: In stiff ventricles (HFpEF, hypertrophic CM), adequate diastolic filling time is critical; tachycardia disproportionately reduces CO.

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: A patient has fever, headache, behavioral change, and temporal lobe findings on MRI. What empiric treatment must be started immediately?
answer: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours empirically for suspected HSV encephalitis (treat for 14-21 days if confirmed).
rationale: HSV encephalitis mortality exceeds 50% untreated; empiric acyclovir must not await PCR confirmation.
confusable_with: Bacterial meningitis (fever + meningismus, treat with antibiotics + dexamethasone)

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: What brain regions does HSV encephalitis typically affect and what are the resulting symptoms?
answer: Temporal and frontal lobes; causes psychiatric features, memory deficits, and aphasia.
rationale: HSV-1 has tropism for limbic structures; temporal lobe involvement manifests as personality change, memory loss, and aphasia rather than focal motor deficits.

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: What is the recommended treatment for CMV encephalitis and its duration?
answer: Ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV every 12 hours + foscarnet 60-90 mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours for 21 days.
rationale: CMV requires combination antiviral therapy; ganciclovir alone has higher resistance rates in immunocompromised patients.

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: What clinical history elements guide viral encephalitis workup?
answer: Immune status, insect/animal exposure, travel history, vaccination history, geography, and season.
rationale: These epidemiologic factors dramatically narrow the differential; e.g. West Nile in summer, rabies with bat exposure, EBV/CMV in immunocompromised.

domain: Internal medicine: neurology (ischemic & hemorrhagic stroke, seizures & status epilepticus, altered mental status & delirium, headache, neuromuscular weakness, spinal cord syndromes)
stem: What ICP complication of viral encephalitis is associated with poor outcomes?
answer: Elevated intracranial pressure; requires serial ICP monitoring and management.
rationale: Brain edema from encephalitis raises ICP, reducing CPP; uncontrolled ICP elevation causes brainstem herniation and death.

enabling_conditions: Immunocompromised (AIDS, transplant, chemo), summer/fall (arbovirus), animal contact (rabies), unvaccinated
pathophysiology: Viral invasion of brain parenchyma causing direct neuronal damage, perivascular inflammation, and cerebral edema
time_course: Acute to subacute; prodrome of fever/headache followed by AMS/behavioral change/seizures over days
key_features: Fever + headache + AMS + behavioral change +/- seizures; HSV: temporal lobe, psychiatric; arbovirus: motor; EBV: splenomegaly
consequence_if_missed: HSV encephalitis untreated: >50% mortality; delayed acyclovir increases death and neurologic morbidity
